articles.title: Ilhan Omar home raid, Haines attack: Inside rise in violence on officials
articles.summary: US Congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s home raided; Australian MP Helen Haines loses both legs following an attack.
articles.body:
United States Congresswoman Ilhan Omar has been forced to move out of her Washington, DC residence because of safety concerns after her home was raided, amid growing threats of violence against politicians.

Last week, US federal agents searched Omar’s home with what a Justice Department spokesperson described as a “judicially authorised search warrant”, adding that the raid was part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation”.

According to NBC News, which cited one person familiar with the matter, charges against Omar may include conspiracy and making false statements in her immigration paperwork.

For years, Somalia-born Omar, who is Muslim, has been the target of right-wing conspiracy theories about her immigration status , including allegations that she had married her brother.

The Minnesota congresswoman has repeatedly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies”.

She has drawn the particular ire of US President Donald Trump, who views her as a thorn in his side and has threatened to deport her.

Omar came to the US in 1995 at age 12 and was naturalised as a US citizen in 2000. Since January 2019, she has served as a congressional representative for the state of Minnesota.

But on Wednesday, she told the US news outlet MS NOW that following the raid on her Washington apartment, she could no longer live there.

“Because our address has been public and with the death threats that I deal with, it’s no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids visiting off and on, having people track them,” she said.

The raid on Omar’s home comes as violent attacks on politicians have grown more frequent.

She, herself, has been physically assaulted. In January this year, Omar was sprayed with an unknown substance by an assailant while calling for the abolition of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency at a town hall meeting in Minneapolis.

On Monday this week, Australian independent MP Helen Haines , who has championed climate action and advocated for improved working conditions as a lawmaker, was hit by a car outside her electorate office, resulting in the amputation of both of her legs.

Australian police said it was a “targeted attack” and warned of growing “online extremism” and recorded a rise in abuse, threats and intimidation targeting lawmakers.

The violent attack on Haines was particularly shocking. Her attacker, identified as Brendan Nugent, 43, allegedly drove past her before turning his car around and veering towards Haines, pinning her against her car.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the driver then reversed before ramming her again.

Sofia Collignon, a reader in comparative politics and director of the Mile End Institute of Research at Queen Mary University London, said instances of physical violence, such as the attack on Haines, are still “relatively rare in terms of numbers”.

“It’s very upsetting to see that more and more people in public life are paying a very high price for doing something that is a public good,” Collignon told Al Jazeera.

Abuse online often comes before physical attacks, however.

She said that women – and, in particular, women of colour in politics – are facing high levels of abuse on social media, and this is taking a worrying toll.

“We are seeing from research that this is having an effect on how they [women] behave in politics, or whether they change the way that they campaign, change the type of issues that they advocate or sometimes completely refrain from participating on social media,” she said.

According to a 2023 report by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), which assessed 12 years of data on attacks against Italian politicians, “marginally elected women are approximately three times more likely to experience an attack” than marginally elected men.

The Princeton School of Public and International Affairs Bridging the Gap initiative, which tracks political violence in the US, found that there has been a “dangerous escalation in the political violence risk environment in the US, including a series of high-profile assassinations and aggressive federal immigration operations”, in 2025

“Incidents of threats and harassment spiked, and leading community safety practitioners reported that the demand for de-escalation support surged to new heights,” it added.

In the case of Omar, Trump has repeatedly targeted the congresswoman since his first term of office over her Somali origins.

He has called her a “sick person”, an “extremist”, and “garbage”, among other inflammatory language.

Other Muslim or progressive congresswomen have also been subjected to Trump’s rhetoric. In February, he wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform that Omar and Palestinian American congresswoman Rashida Tlaib should be sent “back from where they came from”.

But Trump himself has also contended with political violence. In 2024, during his campaign rally, Trump was shot in the ear by a spectator attending the rally.

Then, Trump ally Charlie Kirk was killed in 2025 by a man named Tyler Robinson, who said he had carried out the attack because he had “enough of his [Kirk’s] hatred”.

‘Fierce political polarisation’ to blame

Online threats of attacks on politicians have led to real-life killings for some time.

In 2016, British MP Jo Cox was killed in her constituency while campaigning to remain in the European Union ahead of the referendum by a man named Thomas Mair, who had shouted: “This is for Britain.”

In 2021, Conservative British MP David Amess was killed by a man named Ali Harbi Ali, who claimed that he had targeted the representative over his vote for air strikes on Syria.

In 2026, former Conservative MP and spokesperson for the far-right Reform UK party, Ann Widdecombe, was killed by a man named Joshua Kerry, who has been charged with engaging in conduct in preparation for “acts of terrorism”, including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Collignon said she believes social media has “lowered the bar” for bad-faith actors to threaten politicians, which explains the increase in the volume of threats.

“For example, what people consider to be acceptable ways of referring to politicians or to talk to them are more and more aggressive. They can find it acceptable to use more aggressive terms, partly because of the polarisation in politics,” she said.

“It’s not an issue that we observed only on the right or on the left, but we observe it very often on the fringes of the spectrum. They find that it is acceptable to use unacceptable language or behaviour in the pursuit of their political goals. So that means intimidating a politician is something that they kind of condone.”

According to an Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) 2026 annual report, local officials faced a “persistent and evolving threat of violence in 2025” in an analysis of 2,653 incidents of violence that targeted local officials globally.

The data show that the recorded incidents worldwide have spread from 88 countries and territories in 2025 to 97 in 2024.

“Over the past five years, ACLED records at least 13,900 incidents in 138 countries and territories,” said the report. “Local officials often become lightning rods for broader societal grievances. Large-scale protest movements in recent years have directed their frustration and anger at local authorities, viewed as the nerve endings of a failing or corrupt state.

“Especially in Europe and the United States, a pernicious mix of fierce political polarisation and unchecked competition for political dominance exposes politicians, and especially local elected officials, to a growing trend of harassment, abuse and violence.”

Clionadh Raleigh, ACLED CEO, told Al Jazeera that while public officials can be challenged and voted out, “violence against them should never be ignored or excused”.

“Political violence is not exclusive to the left or right, and both extremes show greater openness to violence. These attacks are not simply isolated threats to individuals, but part of a wider pattern of political intimidation,” Raleigh said.

A 2026 report by the Inter-Parliamentary Union, a global international organisation of national parliaments, revealed that of the 519 parliamentarians who participated in research across five national case studies and joined a global survey, 71 percent of all respondents reported having “experienced violence by the public, whether online, offline or both”.

“Violence is heavily concentrated online, with between 65 percent and 77 percent of MPs across the case studies reporting online abuse,” it found.

However, Collignon said the line between online threats of violence and being physically assaulted has become increasingly blurred.

“Let’s say that I check my social media accounts at home, a place where I should feel safe,” she said. “But then, if my phone is showing me constant abuse, threats of violence, very nasty behaviour, then I am receiving all of these attacks in my living room.

“We currently are operating in a space where lines are blurry, and I think we shouldn’t be thinking about online violence as something that just happens in the digital sphere. It’s something that has consequences for the individual in their daily lives, and the way in which they are involved in politics.”

articles.title: Germany arrests Ukrainian man accused of spying for Russia
articles.summary: Military has raised the threat level of Russian sabotage against German troops and facilities.
articles.body:
A Ukrainian national has been arrested in Germany on suspicion of spying for Russia, German authorities have said.

Germany’s federal prosecutors confirmed in a statement on Thursday that the man, identified as Vadym Y, was arrested in the state of Brandenburg 85km (53 miles) west of Berlin.

Prosecutors said the suspect had been in touch with the Russian secret service via an intermediary since at least July 2025.

The suspect had gathered military intelligence on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as military personnel and defence installations at locations designed to secure NATO’s eastern flank, prosecutors added.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is currently meeting with regional leaders in Montenegro for the EU-Western Balkans Summit, said he was “not surprised” by the news of a suspected Russian spy.

The arrest comes after German authorities blamed Russia for drone attacks that officials said are part of Moscow’s “shadow war” on the country.

Germany’s armed forces on Wednesday raised the threat level of Russian sabotage against their troops and facilities to “significant” for the first time – the ‌second-highest level on their internal threat scale, German news reports noted.

The move followed the discovery in mid-September of a crashed drone carrying high explosives near the Wunstorf ⁠airbase in Lower Saxony, German news sites WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported.

The drone resembled another unmanned aircraft – also laden with explosives – used in a failed attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August. Unlike the Leipzig incident, which authorities said targeted civilian cargo aircraft, investigators believe the Wunstorf drone targeted military aircraft, according to an internal military document seen by German media.

The report also noted a pattern of suspected Russian reconnaissance across Germany, including drones flown over a missile defence site in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, and a camouflaged camera found filming a strategically important railway station in Minden, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Martin Jaeger, head of Germany’s BND spy service, told lawmakers this month that Russia’s undeclared “shadow war” against Germany and its allies was escalating further and has “taken on a new, more dangerous character”.

“Germany is at risk of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia,” he told an intelligence oversight committee at Germany’s parliament, the Bundestag.

Moscow denied involvement and has maintained it is not involved in sabotage or hybrid attacks on European nations.

articles.title: Indian diaspora could pay price for West’s immigration backlash, warns Sushant Sareen
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has blamed immigration for the recent unrest in France and urged President Emmanuel Macron to close the country’s borders,
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has blamed immigration for the recent unrest in France and urged President Emmanuel Macron to close the country’s borders, reigniting a wider debate over migration, integration and the future of Western societies.But the backlash could also hurt Indians who have built successful lives abroad through legal migration, strategic affairs expert Sushant Sareen has warned.“The law breakers don't care anyways but it's the guys who follow the law who will also get crushed,” Sareen said in an interview on Faultline, hosted by Ananya Dasgupta.Trump has described France’s unrest as a consequence of immigration and warned that Europe risks decline unless it tightens its borders. Macron, however, has rejected attempts by foreign leaders to blame migrants for the violence, pointing to the exploitation of France’s domestic tensions for political gain.Why Indians could pay the priceSareen said the Indian diaspora had established a reputation for success in countries such as the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.“The Indian diaspora wherever it went it made a success of itself,” he said.However, he argued that this reputation could come under pressure as anti-immigration sentiment grows. Referring to Canada, Sareen alleged that criminal activity involving some members of the Indian community, including people he linked to Khalistani networks, had damaged the image of the wider diaspora.His concern is that Indians unconnected with such activities could also face the consequences of a broader backlash against migrants.Is the West paying for its own mistakes?Sareen sees the immigration debate as part of a wider crisis facing Western societies. He argued that governments had failed to manage integration and address tensions around migration, leaving established political and social models under strain.“Multiculturalism has collapsed,” he said, describing what he sees as the failure of the Western approach to managing cultural diversity.Yet Western economies continue to need migrant workers, particularly as populations age and employers face labour shortages. Sareen said governments must rethink their immigration systems, including how long migrants can stay and what rights they should have.For Indians hoping to study, work or settle abroad, tougher visa rules could complicate future plans. Those already settled overseas could also face uncertainty if immigration becomes a proxy for wider anxieties about jobs, identity and cultural change.The contradiction is that Western countries need foreign talent even as political pressure to restrict immigration grows.For India, the stakes extend beyond visa policies. If the West responds to its immigration crisis by treating migrant communities as a single group, law-abiding Indians who have contributed to their host countries could find themselves paying the price.Watch Faultlinewith Ananya Dasgupta and Sushant Sareen as they discuss the France crisis, the West’s immigration trap, the growing backlash and why Indians could pay the price.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Netanyahu promises Iran regime change: Can Israel topple Tehran government?
articles.summary: Israel can inflict devastating damage on Iran, but analysts question its ability to overthrow Tehran’s government.
articles.body:
Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that overthrowing Iran’s government remains Israel’s “primary objective”, as he faces declining support in the polls before national elections next week.

His remarks came after conversations with United States President Donald Trump on Sunday and a visit to Israel by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. But Netanyahu offered no indication that Washington had agreed to join another offensive against Iran, let alone a campaign to bring down Iran’s leadership.

While Israel has the firepower to inflict serious damage on Iran, analysts told Al Jazeera, it lacks a clear strategy for translating military gains into the overthrow of Iran’s government. Air strikes alone are unlikely to achieve that objective, while a ground invasion would demand a far greater military commitment, they said.

A renewed offensive would also mean confronting a state that has already survived two rounds of attacks and retains the means to retaliate – both against Israel and its Gulf neighbours who are hosting US military assets. US backing, meanwhile, remains uncertain, with experts questioning Washington’s appetite for renewed fighting as it is yet to find a credible prospect of forcing Iran’s government to surrender to its demands.

Israel’s ability to attack Iran is not in doubt, experts say. Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera that its offensive weapons stockpiles, and “aerial refuelling” capabilities give it a substantial advantage. “Israel could again establish air superiority and strike Iranian targets,” he said.

But while Israel can inflict serious damage, analysts are sceptical that it can accomplish regime change.

Netanyahu has portrayed Iran’s leaders as a major threat since his first term as prime minister in 1996. Addressing the US Congress that July, he said, “The most dangerous of these regimes is Iran, that has wed a cruel despotism to a fanatic militancy.”

Nearly 30 years later, US participation in the June 2025 war, and again in the campaign launched on February 28 this year, delivered the military intervention Netanyahu had long sought. The overthrow of Iran’s government, however, did not follow. Netanyahu himself acknowledged the limits of airpower in March, saying, “You can’t do it only from the air.”

“There has to be a ground component, as well,” he added, without explaining what that would involve.

Caglar Kurc, an assistant professor at Abdullah Gul University in Kayseri, Turkiye, said bombing could weaken Iran’s military but not necessarily eliminate its ability to fight back. “Airpower can degrade military capabilities but cannot fully destroy offensive capabilities,” he told Al Jazeera. “Well-hidden systems would survive.”

Overthrowing the government, Kurc said, would require a willingness to deploy troops and remain on the ground for years. Israel can also no longer assume that covert methods used in earlier attacks would prove equally effective again.

Coningham described intelligence assets as “use and burn” because deploying these methods risks exposing networks that Iranian security services will investigate and disrupt.

Israel still has “human intelligence assets on the ground”, he said, while “cyberattacks” could also form part of another campaign. But using those capabilities risks revealing and sacrificing them, making the prospect of a tangible military gain an important consideration.

Covert operations and cyberattacks, in his assessment, do not offer a clear route to overthrowing Iran’s government. Coningham was similarly sceptical that Kurdish or Baloch armed groups could provide the ground force needed to challenge the state. In March, the Trump administration was said to be actively discussing providing arms to opposition Kurdish groups, according to CNN, which cited Kurdish and US officials. But this never progressed.

“Kurdish groups lacked the military capabilities to take on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC),” he said.

Iran also does not need to match Israel aircraft-for-aircraft to make another offensive very costly, experts say.

Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at RUSI, told Al Jazeera that the “Iranians likely retain sizeable stocks of missiles,” even if damage to their targeting systems may constrain their effectiveness.

“The actual antiship missile stockpiles likely remain large, both because they are comparatively easy to make, and Iran has in-housed much of the production of older Chinese ASCMs, and Iran’s southern mountains provide natural shelters against air attack,” Kaushal said.

Coningham said that, for Israel, sustaining its defences would be more difficult, with previous exchanges having drawn down interceptor stocks.

Repeated attacks also impose a financial burden, as Israel will be intercepting relatively inexpensive Iranian drones with far more costly defensive weapons. Over a prolonged exchange, that imbalance could place further pressure on Israel’s interceptor supplies, while Iran retains the capacity to mass-produce more cheap weapons for a lot longer.

Analysts consider this unlikely, pointing to diverging political interests between Tel Aviv and Washington, with Trump facing pressure to avoid renewed escalation before the US midterm elections.

The Financial Times reported this week that an Israeli proposal for renewed strikes had failed to secure Trump’s approval, although it suggested disagreement about immediate action rather than Washington ruling out future attacks altogether.

Without Trump’s participation, Coningham said, Israel would lack US capabilities for striking deeply buried facilities. These include the 30,000-pound GBU-57 bunker-busting bombs that US B-2 bombers dropped on Iran’s Fordow and Natanz nuclear facilities in June 2025. Designed to penetrate deeply buried targets, the weapons gave Washington an offensive capability Israel could not match on its own.

Coningham also suggested that, if Israel were to attack without US support, Iran might concentrate its retaliation on Israeli territory while avoiding US targets and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.

Such an approach would seek to punish Israel without drawing Washington directly into the fighting, potentially further isolating a country already widely ostracised by the international community amid its genocide in Gaza.

But analysts say the central obstacle that could ultimately prevent Israel from attacking Iran is the gap between its ability to destroy military targets and its capacity to force political change within Iran.

“You cannot change a regime unless you are prepared to deploy troops and stay in the country for some years. Israel cannot control Iran. The United States would not engage in another regime change, which could take decades,” Kurc added.

articles.title: Carney, Erdogan launch ‘strong and resilient’ Canada-Turkiye partnership
articles.summary: On trade, investment and innovation, leaders will work towards conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement.
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have announced the launch of a Canada-Turkiye Strategic Partnership, backed by a three-year action plan.

“In an increasingly complex global security environment, rising geopolitical uncertainties, and evolving humanitarian challenges, a strong and resilient Canada-Turkiye partnership is essential, providing a foundation to mitigate shared threats and capitalise on new opportunities,” said a statement by the two leaders on Thursday.

This comes as Carney is on a two-day visit to Turkiye, seeking to forge a new partnership as Canada looks to reduce its dependence on the United States.

The partnership’s three-year action plan rests on four pillars: trade and investment; defence and security; energy; and ties between people, the statement said.

On trade, investment and innovation, the two leaders agreed to “work toward successful conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement”, it said. They will also expand bilateral trade and investments in priority sectors, including energy supply, defence production, aerospace, and artificial intelligence (AI).

On defence and security, the leaders “underlined their intent to deepen bilateral and multilateral cooperation”. They also agreed to “strengthen cooperation in support of peace and security in the Euro-Atlantic region and beyond including Ukraine, South Caucasus, and the Middle East, in particular Gaza”.

Meanwhile, energy ministers from both countries will work on areas such as liquefied natural gas, nuclear energy and critical minerals.

Speaking to reporters in Ankara alongside Carney on Thursday, Erdogan said the two countries “hope to increase our trade volume, which currently stands at around $3bn, to $5bn initially and then to $10bn through the steps we will take”.

He said the two sides had agreed to begin free trade agreement negotiations before the end of the year to boost trade and investment, adding that elevating Turkiye-Canada relations to the level of a strategic partnership would not be merely a symbolic step on paper.

Canadian and Turkish leaders will convene next month in Ankara for the first round of trade talks, the joint statement said.

“We have today overcome the disconnect that had persisted between Turkiye and Canada for many years. Now, we are launching a new era between Turkiye and Canada,” Erdogan said.

Relations between the two countries will expand “for generations to come”, Carney said alongside Erdogan.

“Our goal is not self-sufficiency; it is collective resilience, and that’s why Canada is building deeper partnerships with reliable partners that create new opportunities for us both, and in Turkiye, we have an exceptional partner,” he added.

Carney is on the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkiye, although he travelled to Ankara in July to attend the NATO summit.

He was scheduled to meet Erdogan and other officials before travelling to Istanbul for talks with Turkish business groups as the two countries seek to deepen trade ties.

The Canadian prime minister has sought to diversify partnerships and reduce reliance on the US amid an escalating trade war with US President Donald Trump, marked by US tariffs on Canadian goods, followed by retaliatory measures from Canada, as well as Trump’s statements questioning Canadian sovereignty.

articles.title: Washington foster parents score legal victory after state demanded they use children's preferred pronouns
articles.summary: Shane and Jennifer DeGross fought Washington state's foster care gender identity policies after the requirements clashed with their Christian faith.
articles.body: A Christian couple who spent more than a decade caring for foster children is celebrating a major legal victory after Washington state agreed to change its licensing rules following a dispute over requirements that foster parents use children's preferred pronouns and comply with gender identity policies, even when those requirements conflicted with their religious beliefs. Shane and Jennifer DeGross told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday that the dispute began in 2022, when they attempted to renew their foster care license and discovered the state had changed its requirements concerning gender identity. The couple said they were willing to love and care for any child placed in their home but could not agree to certain state-imposed requirements they believed violated their Christian faith. "We were made aware that the state had updated and changed some of their requirements," Jennifer DeGross told Fox News Digital. "While we agreed that we would love and care for any child in our home, they had specific things that we could not agree to as Christians." DOJ BACKS NUNS CARING FOR DYING CANCER PATIENTS IN FIGHT AGAINST NEW YORK TRANS IDEOLOGY MANDATE Shane DeGross said the state required them to affirm the state's views on gender identity and human sexuality. "Those views directly conflict with the biblical worldview of human sexuality," Shane DeGross said. "So, as Christians, we just couldn't accept that. Our allegiance is to God and the truth of Scripture. And we just couldn't abide by what they were requiring us to affirm." Washington's licensing policies required foster parents to affirm and support LGBTQ children, including expectations concerning gender identity and the use of preferred names and pronouns. The DeGross family challenged the requirements on religious freedom grounds. Jennifer said the state eventually partially reinstated their license but restricted the ages of children they could foster. AUTISM PROVIDERS WARN FOSTER KIDS AT RISK FROM UNINTENDED CONSEQUENCES OF TRUMP'S MEDICAID FRAUD CRACKDOWN "We felt like even when they reinstated a partial license to us that they were still discriminating against us," she said. "When a child reached 5, they had to be removed from our home," Jennifer said. "So not only was that upsetting to us, but that's not good for kids, right?" Jennifer argued that such a restriction could disrupt a child's placement even if the child had already spent years living with a foster family. PATRIOTS RB TREVEYON HENDERSON SLAMS STATE OVERREACH AFTER CATHOLIC FAMILY LOSES CUSTODY IN GENDER CASE "If we had had a child for a couple of years, and then they have to be removed just because they turned or reached a certain age, it's definitely not in the interest of children," she said. The legal battle resulted in a settlement under which Washington agreed to revise its foster care licensing rules, addressing the conflict between the state's gender identity requirements and foster parents' religious freedom claims. Johannes Widmalm-Delphonse, senior counsel at Alliance Defending Freedom, told Fox News Digital that the DeGross' case should serve as a lesson for the rest of the country. "These foster care agencies, they have to respect the First Amendment rights of foster parents, as well as the children in the system and everyone that they work with," Widmalm-Delphonse said. "So, states should be on notice from this settlement, as well as some of the other cases that we've seen like the Bates v. Pakseresht decision, that they have to respect First Amendment rights, they have to respect free speech rights, and the way you do that is you invite as many foster parents into the system as possible on the front end, and then you match at the back end according to children's individual needs or family's abilities, comfort level, things like that, which is what they've been doing for decades, and this settlement shows that they can continue doing that now," Widmalm-Delphonse added. WASHINGTON FATHER SUES SCHOOL DISTRICT FOR DENYING RELIGIOUS OPT-OUT FOR 5TH GRADER FROM LGBTQ INSTRUCTION Widmalm-Delphonse said that since the settlement, Washington State has a new proposed regulation, WSR 26-20-103, currently undergoing the public notice and comment process which would in part give foster parents like Shane and Jennifer DeGross a religious exemption. "This new rule, in part, would give foster parents like the DeGross's a religious exemption from any rule requiring them to violate their religious beliefs on gender or sexuality," Widmalm-Delphonse said. Shane DeGross told Fox News Digital, "It's a great victory in the sense that more Christians can be available to love and care for foster kids without fear of being excluded because of their religious beliefs." "It's a huge victory for kids that need a loving home," he added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We are proud of the diversity of our foster parent and kinship caregiver community who have different cultures, religious beliefs, and lived experience," the Washington State Department of Children, Youth, and Families said in a news release on the settlement. "We are grateful that they all open their doors and provide a loving home to children and youth in foster care." "This settlement agreement respects the religious beliefs of foster parents, while ensuring LGBTQIA+ youth are placed in an environment that is safe and supports their well-being," DCYF Secretary Tana Senn said. articles.title: A British man spent 11 years building a World War II-style bunker under his garden, adding a 35-foot escape tunnel and a hidden beer lift, with the construction budget expected to reach £35,000
articles.summary: A British man has spent 11 years turning the garden of his Derbyshire home into an underground space inspired by World War II escape tunnels.
articles.body: A British man has spent 11 years turning the garden of his Derbyshire home into an underground space inspired by World War II escape tunnels. Dave Billings, 43, has built two bunkers connected by a 35-foot passage, along with a lift disguised as a beer keg to carry drinks underground. By October 2024, he had spent around £30,000 on the project and expected the final construction cost to reach £35,000.According to The Sun's report, the underground rooms weren't yet connected to his bungalow, but Billings had plans to change that. He wants to create a concealed entrance inside his home, allowing him to reach the bunkers without stepping outside. The proposed route would eventually lead through the tunnel and back into the garden through an old well.For Billings, a fabricator, the project began with an interest in the history of his property. His home stands on land that was once part of a World War II army base. He had hoped to discover an existing bunker there, but when he found none, he decided to build one.“I’ve always wanted to find a bunker on the property, but when I didn’t I thought I’ll build one myself. It’s a bit of a childhood dream, really,” he told DerbyWorld.Small underground room becomes larger projectThe first stage of construction began around 2013. At the time, the garden contained an old well, which Billings incorporated into his plans. He constructed stairs leading down to a bunker measuring approximately 13 square metres.For several years, this was the main underground space on the property. But Billings eventually decided that he wanted something bigger. In 2023, he began work on a second bunker, this time with approximately 25 square metres of space.He decided to connect it to the existing bunker. This meant digging a tunnel stretching 35 feet between the two structures.The idea came partly from The Great Escape, the 1963 film based on the escape of Allied prisoners of war from Stalag Luft III during World War II. The prisoners had dug underground passages in an attempt to escape captivity. Billings wanted to recreate the appearance of those tunnels, including wooden lining along the passage.A hidden entrance and an unusual way to deliver beerThe tunnel is only one part of the underground arrangement Billings hoped to create. His longer-term plan involved extending his bungalow closer to the bunker and installing a secret door that would provide access from inside the house.This would make it possible to enter the underground rooms from the bungalow, move through the connecting passage and return to the surface through the well.Billings also wanted visitors to be able to use the underground route without disturbing other people in the house.There is already another feature designed to make life below ground more convenient. Carrying drinks down the stairs proved difficult, so Billings constructed a lift that resembles a beer barrel.The device allows him to lower drinks into the bunker without having to carry them down himself. It is among the more unusual additions to a project that began as a simple underground shelter.Construction costs and plans for finished bunkerDespite carrying out the construction himself, Billings has spent a substantial amount on materials. According to The Sun, around £4,000 went towards bricks, while concrete, waterproofing and insulation added to the overall cost.His decision to do much of the work without hiring builders has helped reduce expenses. He also prepared the designs using Computer-aided design, with a structural engineer checking the specifications.By October 2024, the project had cost approximately £30,000. Billings estimated that completing the new bunker would bring the total to around £35,000.Billings also planned to install a projector and gaming simulator, along with other electronic devices.One of his ideas involved a remote-controlled fridge that could travel towards a person carrying a beer. At the time of the reports, he had not worked out how to make the device.Billings was aiming to finish the larger bunker by Christmas 2024, although he did not expect the project to end there. He was already considering further additions, including the possibility of another tunnel. “It’ll never be fully finished. I’ll always be adding new inventions and maybe even another tunnel,” he said, as quoted by DerbyWorld.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Four London councils challenge government funding reforms
articles.summary: Three Tory and one Liberal Democrat-led councils are officially challenging government funding changes.
articles.body:
Four London council leaders have formally submitted a challenge to government reforms that are set to see their central funding slashed by up to 58%.

The leaders of Wandsworth, Richmond, Westminster and Kensington and Chelsea councils delivered revised funding proposals to the Treasury on Thursday urging the government to rethink its overhaul of local authority funding rules.

Among those councils, the leaders said the reforms would result in funding cuts ranging from 40% to 58% by 2029.

The government said the "outdated" local authority funding model was being reformed to ensure "money goes where it is most needed".

The changes, known as the Fair Funding Review 2.0, aim to shift more cash towards areas with higher deprivation.

Wandsworth's Conservative administration said the reforms would cut funding by 40% and force it to slash services and raise council tax.

The authority is proposing to raise council tax by 94% from April, in addition to making sweeping cuts – including shutting its cost-of-living reserve with £6.2m of unspent funds, replacing Labour's Access for All with a much smaller concessionary scheme, cancelling its Borough of Sanctuary status and suspending voluntary sector grants for four years.

Kensington and Chelsea is set to lose £108m, or more than 40% of its central funding over the next four years under the reforms, while Westminster is due to see these resources drop by around £100m (46%). Richmond is set to be stripped of £26m (58%) of its core funding.

The councils have now formally submitted their revised funding proposals, under the Sustainable Communities Act, asking the government to reconsider its decision.

Wandsworth Council leader Robert Morritt, who heads a Conservative minority administration, said: "Residents should not have to pick up the bill for changes imposed by Whitehall. This proposal takes our case directly to government.

"We are using every route available to fight for a fairer deal and protect Wandsworth taxpayers."

London councils face £5bn gap by 2030, group warns

Westminster council cuts 520 jobs in savings plan

Mixed council verdicts on new 'fair funding' plan

Lib Dem Richmond council leader Gareth Roberts said the cuts risked "pushing this council towards a financial cliff edge".

He said: "We will not stand by while Whitehall forces our residents to pay the price for a deeply flawed formula."

Tory Kensington and Chelsea council leader Elizabeth Campbell said: "I will use every tool at my disposal to fight these cuts, stand up for our residents and secure the fair deal our borough deserves."

A Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government spokesperson previously said: "We have consulted extensively on reforming the outdated council funding system to ensure money goes where it is most needed, following on from a longstanding consensus.

"We're also protecting councils through transitional arrangements so no area faces a cliff edge."

articles.title: CEC impeachment: Speaker Om Birla says fresh motion against Gyanesh Kumar will be examined as per rules
articles.summary: Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said any fresh motion seeking the impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar would be examined
articles.body: Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said any fresh motion seeking the impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar would be examined in accordance with parliamentary rules and procedures, as opposition protests demanding the poll panel chief’s removal intensified over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The opposition has made two attempts to remove Kumar, with notices in the first attempt rejected by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. Notices submitted in the second attempt are still pending in the Upper House.“If any fresh notice comes, we will see and examine it accordingly under rules and procedures,” Birla told a press conference, responding to a question on the possibility of another impeachment motion against the CEC.Protests against Kumar have intensified over the past fortnight, with opposition parties demanding his resignation over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls. The agitation gathered momentum after The Indian Express reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR, alleging that these were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.Under the Constitution, the CEC can be removed only through a parliamentary process similar to that prescribed for the removal of a Supreme Court judge. The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, also provides for the CEC or an Election Commissioner to resign by submitting a written resignation to the President.The removal process is governed by constitutional provisions and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. Once a removal motion is admitted in either House of Parliament, the Speaker or the Rajya Sabha Chairman constitutes a three-member committee to investigate the charges. The panel comprises the Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge, a chief justice of a high court and a distinguished jurist.If the committee finds the charges unsubstantiated, no further action is taken. If it finds the allegations proved, the motion is taken up for consideration in Parliament. Removal requires each House to pass an address supported by a majority of its total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, in the same session.The opposition’s attempts to remove Kumar have brought the Election Commission’s handling of the SIR under renewed scrutiny, with the possibility of another motion now hinging on the formal parliamentary process and the admissibility of any fresh notice.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Controversial substation at Weston Marsh approved by one vote
articles.summary: Opponents say the scheme near Spalding will turn the countryside into an "industrial eyesore".
articles.body:
Plans for an electricity substation in Lincolnshire have been narrowly approved by councillors despite concerns about the impact on the local area.

South Holland District Council's planning committee voted six to five in favour of National Grid's application for a 400kV substation at Weston Marsh, near Spalding, with two abstentions.

The substation is part of the Grimsby to Walpole power line project, which includes 87 miles (140km) of pylons across Lincolnshire to strengthen the UK's electricity network.

Local residents and some councillors objected to the plans, arguing they would destroy high-quality farmland, harm the landscape and increase traffic on narrow rural roads.

Speaking at a meeting on Wednesday, committee chairman James Avery acknowledged the scheme was deemed as "critical national infrastructure", adding many of the concerns were not strong enough to warrant a refusal on planning grounds.

However, he said the scheme was "hugely unpopular" with residents.

Councillor Andrew Woolf said it could turn the countryside into an "industrial eyesore" and create traffic problems during construction.

He added that he understood the "need for renewable energy", but argued the substation was in the wrong location.

Craig Rivett, for National Grid, acknowledged the concerns, but said any impact could be mitigated.

"Biodiversity net gain will be provided and construction and traffic impacts will be appropriately managed through the planning conditions," he said.

Campaign group Lincolnshire Against Needless Destruction (LAND) said it was disappointed by the decision.

Cat Makinson, from the group, said: "The fact that approval was secured by just one vote illustrates how divided the committee was."

As part of the approval, councillors added restrictions on construction hours, including a ban on Sunday and bank holiday working.

articles.title: JJ Watt signs a multiyear deal to stay as CBS’ lead NFL analyst
articles.summary: JJ Watt thought the call he was getting from David Berson on Monday was about potentially breaking Jim Nantz’s hand while doing a demonstration during the Buffalo Bills-Las Vegas Raiders game.
articles.body: JJ Watt thought the call he was getting from David Berson on Monday was about potentially breaking Jim Nantz’s hand while doing a demonstration during the Buffalo Bills-Las Vegas Raiders game. Not only did Nantz turn out to be fine, although a bit sore, but the Chairman of CBS’ and Skydance’s Sports Division had better news to deliver. He was making Watt the permanent lead analyst for CBS Sports’ NFL coverage. The announcement was made Thursday morning along with Watt signing a multiyear agreement. “It’s an incredible honor and it’s humbling,” Watt said in a video he posted on social media. “There’s only five seats that get to do this. I appreciate their trust in me and I have an absolute blast doing it every single week and I cannot wait to continue to do it.” Watt joined play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson after Tony Romo went on leave following his July 23 arrest in Wisconsin. The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback pleaded no contest to charges of operating a vehicle while intoxicated. CBS announced on Oct. 2 that Romo would not return after the two sides “agreed to part ways.” Romo had been the lead game analyst for CBS’ NFL coverage since 2017. Watt and Nantz have already had some memorable moments in the booth. Last week, Watt was showing how players try to protect the football from defensive players attempting the “Peanut Punch,” which is named after former defensive back Charles “Peanut” Tillman. Nantz tried to knock the ball from Watt, but hit his wrist hard on the football and immediately grabbed his hand. Nantz had an ice pack on after halftime and joked that he broke his wrist, but said during interviews this week nothing was broken. Nantz is probable to be in the booth with Watt for Sunday’s game between the Cincinnati Bengals and Baltimore Ravens. “I’ve had a front-row seat to JJ’s growth as a top-tier broadcaster, watching him tackle this role just like he did his hall-of-fame playing career,” Berson said in a statement. “He’s insightful, entertaining, passionate, meticulous in his preparation, and the ultimate teammate. He has a unique ability to see things and communicate to fans of all levels. We are thrilled to have him leading our NFL coverage.” Watt joined CBS Sports in 2023 as a studio analyst on “The NFL Today” following a 12-year career with the Houston Texans and Arizona Cardinals. He was a three-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year, a five-time All-Pro selection and the 2017 Walter Payton NFL Man of the Year. Watt moved to the booth in 2025 and called games on the No. 2 team with Ian Eagle and Evan Washburn before being moved up to the top team this season. He is only the fourth CBS analyst since 1981. Hall of Famer John Madden held the post from 1981 through 1993, when the network lost the rights to the NFL. Phil Simms moved into the spot when CBS got the rights back in 1998 until 2016 and was followed by Romo. Watt will also be in the booth when CBS carries Super Bowl 62 in Atlanta in February 2028. “I’ll see you on Sunday and I’ll see you at the Super Bowl next year,” Watt said to close the video.

articles.title: Italy and Spain lift border controls after months of tension over Ceuta
articles.summary: More than 70,000 people entered Ceuta irregularly from Morocco, triggering border security concerns in the EU bloc.
articles.body:
Italy and Spain have agreed to lift border controls on each ⁠other’s citizens, ending a ⁠three-month standoff triggered after a mass surge of migrants and asylum seekers entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.

The Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi and his Spanish counterpart Fernando Grande-Marlaska ⁠spoke on the phone and agreed not to extend ⁠their suspension of the ⁠European Union’s open-border Schengen arrangements, an Italian statement said on Thursday.

“The decision, reached after a careful assessment of ‌the situation, will be accompanied by enhanced information-sharing measures to ensure the full security ‌of ‌the common Schengen area,” the ministry added.

The decision followed a meeting between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on the sidelines of a European Council meeting.

Italy’s right-wing government first suspended its open-border arrangements ‌with Spain on July 31, saying it wanted to make sure no migrants entering the North African enclave of Ceuta could travel to Italian territory.

Madrid responded by taking similar action against Rome, describing the ⁠Italian measures as “unjust, contrary ⁠to European Union interests, and discriminatory to the population of Spain”.

The tit-for-tat border closures happened after upwards of 70,000 people swam around barricades and entered Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco on July 30 and 31, fuelling tension in the Spanish territory.

Most returned to Morocco within hours, but thousands, including unaccompanied minors, have remained for weeks in often dire conditions .

“We thought our government was going to do something in the short or medium term, but we’ve been here for two months, and these people haven’t been sent back,” Ceuta resident Ruben Gonzalez said.

The Spanish government’s handling of the mass crossing of migrants into Ceuta has complicated Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s bid for re-election in November.

Sanchez was already facing criticism for his government’s decision to open a path to legal status for hundreds of thousands of undocumented foreign residents.

After the Ceuta incident, Far-right Vox and centre-right PP parties accused him of being soft on immigration and put the issue at the centre of their campaigns in the run-up to next month’s elections.

articles.title: Israeli attacks in Gaza kill four, including a young girl
articles.summary: Four Palestinians killed as Israeli military expands control across Gaza, displacing millions and destroying homes.
articles.body:
Israeli attacks across Gaza have killed four Palestinians, including a child, in the past 24 hours as the Israeli military continues to expand its control inside the territory.

The deaths included a young girl who was killed by Israeli gunfire in northern Gaza near the Jabalia refugee camp, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting from Gaza City, said a strike on a vehicle in Gaza City’s Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood killed one person and seriously injured another.

A separate strike killed a man on a bicycle in the southern city of Khan Younis.

Meanwhile, the Gaza Health Ministry reported that a fourth person had died on Thursday of wounds sustained earlier in an Israeli strike.

Along with the deadly attacks , the Israeli military continues to grab more land inside Gaza. Close to two million people live in what remains of the shrinking territory, which is littered with thousands of tonnes of rubble and debris.

“Israel is expanding their control inside Gaza,” Mahmoud explained, noting that Israeli troops have been “taking more land since the ceasefire” and expanding from northern Gaza inward to the centre and westward.

“People cannot return to their homes, and most buildings in the areas Israel controls have been left in ruins,” the reporter said.

Al Jazeera’s maps have shown that nearly two-thirds of Gaza is under Israeli military control or subject to access restrictions.

At least 1,538 Palestinians have been killed and 5,498 injured since the “ceasefire” took effect in October last year, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.

Israel has killed more than 74,400 Palestinians in Gaza since October 2023.

articles.title: Two Syrian security officers killed in raid on ISIL cell near Damascus
articles.summary: The Syrian Interior Ministry says five suspected fighters killed and six arrested outside of Damascus.
articles.body:
Two members of Syria’s internal security forces have been killed and five wounded in clashes with a suspected ISIL (ISIS) cell during a raid on the outskirts of Damascus, the Interior Ministry reported.

The fighting began on Thursday morning, when security forces launched an operation against the cell in the town of Rankous in the western Damascus countryside. The operation is the latest in a series of raids as the government tries to dismantle ISIL networks and prevent attacks.

The ministry said the suspects refused to surrender and opened fire, triggering the clashes. Five alleged ISIL members were killed and six arrested, and weapons and explosive belts were seized.

Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett, reporting from Syria, said residents told her the clashes began around 6am (03:00 GMT) and lasted two to three hours. Some of the wounded security personnel were seriously hurt, she said.

Residents said the group was about nine people – smaller than what officials reported – with two members killed, another two escaping, and an unknown number injured.

Residents told the local outlet Syria Now that security forces imposed a curfew and arrested several people.

The ministry also reportedly foiled an ISIL plot in the Damascus countryside and dismantled an ISIL cell in the Houla area of Homs earlier this month. The plots involved attacking places of worship and security patrols, according to Syria Now.

On October 6, the ministry announced the arrest of Khaled Raed Birouni, also known as Abu Hassan Dushka, in the town of Hujaira in the Damascus countryside. Authorities say he was the group’s top military commander for Homs.

They accused him of planning several attacks there, including the December 2025 bombing of a mosque in the city’s Wadi al-Dhahab neighbourhood during Friday prayers, which killed eight people and wounded 18, according to Syria’s Health Ministry.

ISIL has repeatedly attacked Syrian security forces, usually targeting buses and vehicles carrying personnel, Pett said, along with a few attacks on civilians.

Syria joined the 90-member international coalition against ISIL in November, six years after Syrian Kurdish-led forces led the territorial defeat of ISIL strongholds in the country’s northeast.

articles.title: Map thief led court on 'merry dance' with return promises
articles.summary: The 1684 world map, cut from an atlas at the National Maritime Museum’s library, has not been found.
articles.body:
A man who used a Stanley knife to cut a rare 17th Century world map out of an atlas at a museum library has been jailed for three years.

Melvin West, 70, sliced the map from a 1684 atlas by Dutch cartographer Frederik de Wit while viewing it at the Caird Library, part of the National Maritime Museum in Greenwich, in February 2025.

The map has never been found, and a judge at Woolwich Crown Court said West had led the court, police and museum a "merry dance" over where it was.

The Metropolitan Police has appealed for anyone who knows where it is to come forward.

The double hemisphere world map, known as Nova Orbis Tabula, was one of 12 in the atlas, and is studied by scholars around the world.

The court heard West, from Chingford in east London, had viewed the atlas on 19 and 20 December 2024 and again on the day before the theft.

Staff called police after finding a knife on the floor of the viewing room where he had been looking at the atlas. They then discovered the map had been cut out.

West was arrested at his home in March 2025, but the map was not there. He pleaded guilty at Bromley Magistrates' Court in May to theft, criminal damage and possession of a bladed article.

Prosecution barrister Damian Warburton said the complete atlas had been worth about £50,000 and the map alone could fetch £6,000 on the black market.

The atlas is now valued at £20,000, but he told the court the "cultural loss far outweighs the financial loss".

Defence barrister Jessica Flain said West had partly paid a man to restore the map, but he would not hand it back until the full fee was settled. She asked for sentencing to be adjourned for seven days so a friend could pay the balance and West could take the map to Charing Cross Police Station.

Judge Charlotte Welsh refused, saying she did "not believe a word of it".

She said West had told the court in June that he could return the map within seven days, and in August that it was with a friend and he would retrieve it once he had recovered from heart surgery.

"Again, that appears to have been a lie," she said. "You were charged in February. You have had eight months to return the map."

The judge said she believed West had a buyer in mind and had stolen the map "to order".

The court heard he had 27 convictions for 107 offences in the UK and abroad, mostly for dishonesty and including 41 thefts. They included a burglary conviction in Hungary in 2011 and a theft conviction in France in 2013, and he had also been convicted under various identities.

Flain said West, a father of two, was "ashamed and embarrassed" and had been in debt and unable to meet basic living costs. She described the offence as "a short-term, pressured decision by an elderly man living in difficult circumstances".

Judge Welsh said the map was of "international cultural significance" and the damage had "permanently diminished what can be learned from it". The court was told the two digital copies of the atlas are incomplete.

West was jailed for three years for criminal damage, with concurrent sentences of 16 months for theft and six months for possessing a bladed article. The judge refused to suspend the sentence, saying immediate custody was needed "to deter other people from doing precisely what you have".

articles.title: Meet Rami Rifi, the 16-year-old Staten Island student who turned a closet clean-out into a project supplying new shoes to children in need
articles.summary: Rami Rifi, a Staten Island teenager and founder of the Play Passion Project, is a young philanthropist providing new shoes to children in need through a
articles.body: Rami Rifi, a Staten Island teenager and founder of the Play Passion Project, is a young philanthropist providing new shoes to children in need through a youth-led nonprofit shoe drive. What began as a wardrobe clear-out has grown into a charitable footwear donation initiative serving schoolchildren, families and communities in New York and across the world. Built by a high school junior, the student-led giving movement collects new and lightly worn pairs, then places them directly with children who need them. It stands as a practical model of teenage community service and ethical charity, powered by dedicated volunteers and local vendors.How unworn shoes, profit-driven donation bins and one teenager's question sparked a New York nonprofitRifi, who attends Staten Island Academy, was clearing out his closet when the idea took shape. He told ABC7NY that the shoes he no longer wore were in good quality and he did not want to throw them away. According to the Play Passion Project website, he found 32 pairs, then looked into donating them and discovered that most donation bins near him are run for profit. Shoes left there would feed a resale pipeline instead of reaching someone who needed them. That gap between what donors intend and where their gifts actually end up became the reason the organisation exists.From 1,500 pairs in three weeks to 80,000 pairs: how the Play Passion Project shoe drives scaled upThe first shoe drive followed soon afterwards and gathered 1,500 pairs in just three weeks, far more than anyone had expected from a first attempt. Rather than simply collecting more, the team set out to build a direct line between the person giving and the person receiving. Within the first 12 months, the drives had moved 40,000 pairs. The organisation now reports that 80,000 pairs have reached people who needed them.The Public School 74 surprise was that every pupil received new sneakers, snow boots and dress shoesAhead of the winter break, ABC7NY reported that a gym at Public School 74 became a surprise shoe shop. Every pupil left with new sneakers, snow boots, dress shoes and slides. Rifi planned the send-off with local vendors who filled goodie bags, and children from each grade paraded past Santa before collecting their pairs. Principal Susan Mazzeo told the station that about 50 pupils at the school live in shelters and that it serves a high-poverty community, so any joy the project could bring was welcome. For Rifi, the gesture goes beyond footwear. "The shoes represent dignity, confidence, having something comfortable to walk in, even," he said.How a kindergartener's dinosaur boots inspired the Youth Empowerment Program for student organisersOne moment during that first year changed the organisation's direction, the Play Passion Project website explains. A kindergarten pupil named Gilbert donated his favourite pair of dinosaur boots, and they eventually reached a boy named Christopher in Guatemala. A single pair of shoes connected two children who never met. The episode convinced the team that young people are best placed to carry the work forward, which led to the Youth Empowerment Program. It says the programme has empowered 455 students across four states, training them to run drives, manage logistics and lead in their own communities.The community partners and awards behind the Play Passion Project shoe nonprofit across New York CityThe organisation appears at community events alongside the New York City Police Department. It also works with the Staten Island Giving Circle, Seaman's Society, Soles4Souls, Safe Horizon and a growing list of nonprofits and schools. Its work has drawn public recognition, including a Congressional Gold Medal and a feature as NY1's New Yorker of the Week. The mission remains deliberately simple: put shoes on the feet of people in need while giving the younger generation the means to make that happen.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: These 19+ gifts for music lovers hit all the right notes
articles.summary: Shop the best gifts for music lovers, from headphones and record players to instruments and stocking stuffers, with picks from NBC Selected editors.
articles.body: Music lovers can be surprisingly tricky to shop for. Whether they spend their weekends digging through crates at the record store, practicing guitar every night or simply can’t leave the house without headphones, music aficionados often already own the basics, and the gear they want next tends to be specific. A thoughtful gift can still hit the right note: an upgrade to their listening setup, something that helps them make music of their own or a fun accessory that celebrates their favorite artists. To help you find something they’ll actually use, I gathered gift ideas for music fans of all ages, including options for adults and kids. I sourced items NBC Selected editors love, and I also pulled standout picks from popular brands we’ve covered before. Below, you’ll find headphones and speakers, turntables, instruments, stocking stuffers and more. Best music gifts for adults The AirPods 5 are a great gift for music lovers who listen on the go and pretty much anywhere else. They have up to 1.5 times more noise cancellation than the previous generation, adaptive audio that adjusts to your surroundings and up to 22 hours of total battery life with the USB-C wireless charging case. NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans, who received a pair from the brand, also says they fit more comfortably than previous models: “I was pleasantly surprised that these pods with no rubber eartip didn’t budge.” These earbuds are a great pick for Android users, especially those with a Galaxy phone. They support 24-bit hi-res audio and have a two-way speaker for richer sound, plus upgraded active noise cancellation to block out distractions. They’re also IP57-rated for dust and water resistance, and they come with interchangeable ear tips for a snug, comfortable fit. Guitar Center offers lessons for a wide range of instruments, including guitar (electric and acoustic), bass, drums, keyboard, and even voice, so your recipient can pick whichever one excites them most. They also get to choose the day and time that fits their schedule and the instructor they like, making it easy to start playing. Just load the gift card with an amount you think makes sense to get them started — you can pick from one of the preset amounts up to $1,000 or put in a custom amount — then deliver it via email, text, Messenger or Whatsapp. The Soundcore Life Q30 headphones are a great budget-friendly gift for anyone who prefers over-ear headphones, with many of the features you’d find on pricier pairs. They have active noise cancellation, transparency mode, a folding design and a hard case for travel. But the real standout is the battery life, with up to 40 hours of playback with noise cancellation on and 60 hours with it off. And you get all of this for well under $100. Help a loved one bring their playlists everywhere with this portable speaker. The compact speaker has a built-in carabiner, so you can clip it to a backpack, belt loop or beach bag. It’s also IP67 dustproof and waterproof, gets up to 12 hours of battery life and can pair with other compatible JBL speakers for bigger sound. Evans says that this was her favorite portable speaker until her husband clipped it to his golf bag and she never saw it again. “And just like that, it became his favorite portable speaker,” she says. This ticket stub organizer is a great pick for the sentimental people who never throw out a concert ticket. The binder holds up to 80 tickets in 20 acid-free plastic pages, each with lined inserts where they can jot down memories from the show, like the setlist or who they went with. A pocket inside the back cover stores programs and other keepsakes. This Victrola suitcase record player is a fun, beginner-friendly pick for anyone just starting a vinyl collection. The three-speed turntable plays 33, 45 and 78 RPM records through built-in stereo speakers, and you can also stream music from your phone via Bluetooth. It packs up into a retro-style suitcase with a carrying handle, and it has a headphone jack for private listening. In “The Uncool,” Oscar-winning filmmaker Cameron Crowe looks back on his teenage years as a rock journalist, when he became Rolling Stone’s youngest-ever contributor at 15. The memoir chronicles the real-life events that inspired “Almost Famous,” including his time with Led Zeppelin, the Allman Brothers and David Bowie, and also covers films like “Fast Times at Ridgemont High” and “Jerry Maguire.” The Echo Dot is an affordable way to fill a bedroom, office or dining room with music. Just ask Alexa to play songs from streaming services like Amazon Music, Apple Music and Spotify, and the compact speaker delivers vibrant sound. It also works with Alexa+, Amazon’s upgraded AI assistant, and can control compatible smart home devices. These DuoMuo coasters look like tiny vinyl records, with retro album-style designs that make for a fun conversation starter when guests come over. The set of six comes with a whimsical holder shaped like a record player, so they double as decor on a coffee table, shelf or bar cart, even when they’re not in use. A StubHub gift card is an easy way to treat someone to live music. Recipients can put it toward tickets to concerts, as well as sports games, theater and other live events, so they can pick a show they’re excited about. StubHub gift cards don’t expire, so there’s no pressure to use it before their favorite artist announces a tour. Hitster is a music party game where players scan a card with the free Hitster app to play a song on Spotify, then guess when it was released and place it on their timeline. The first to correctly place 10 songs wins. The game includes more than 300 hits spanning the last 100 years and works for two to 10 players. Tiny Vinyl makes mini 4-inch records that have one song on each side. This one featuring Bob Marley & The Wailers is a fun stocking stuffer for record collectors. It has “Three Little Birds” on one side and “Sun Is Shining” on the other, and it plays on most manual turntables. Tiny Vinyl is sold exclusively at Target and you can get a number of other artists, as well — including Ariana Grande, Noah Kahan, and Katseye. Lola’s portable CD player brings back the joy of listening to an album start to finish. The silver player has anti-skip protection so music won’t cut out on the go, up to 48 hours of battery life and a micro SD card slot for extra music. Evans, who tested this player, says another huge plus is that it doesn’t rely on WiFi or connectivity, so you can literally listen to it anywhere without worrying about buffering. It comes with polka dot earphones, though it works with any wired headphones. Loop Experience 2 earplugs are a thoughtful gift for concertgoers, musicians and festival fans. They reduce noise by 17 decibels while keeping music sounding clear, so the recipient can protect their hearing without missing out on the show. They come with four sizes of silicone ear tips for a comfortable fit, and a carrying case. They’re also nearly invisible from the front. Best music gifts for kids This small piano is a great first instrument for young music lovers — I know because my 5-year-old daughter is obsessed with it. The 37-key digital piano has velocity-sensitive keys, built-in speakers and a rechargeable battery that lasts about eight hours. It also comes with flashcards and pairs with a learning app featuring video lessons and songs. I like that it’s compact and easy to tuck away when she’s done playing. This mini karaoke machine is a fun gift for kids who love to sing. It comes with two wireless microphones, so they can duet with their favorite singing partner, and it connects to a phone or tablet via Bluetooth to play songs from any music app. It also has four voice-changing effects and is small enough to fit in a backpack. The Yoto Player lets kids listen to music, stories and podcasts without a screen. They just pop in a Yoto Card or twist the new Green Button to play one of their favorites. The 4th-gen model has acoustically engineered stereo sound, a night light and an okay-to-wake clock, and you can make custom cards with your own playlists or recordings. Introduce toddlers to real music skills with this set, which includes six instruments, including pat bells, a pan flute and a concertina, plus a working metronome. Every instrument uses the pentatonic scale, so whatever kids play sounds harmonious. A color-coded rhythm and songs book teaches them to play simple tunes, and a play guide offers tips for each stage from 18 months to 4 years old. This 360-piece Lego set lets Olivia Rodrigo fans build a vinyl record decorated with nods to her career, including a megaphone, red lips, a butterfly and an autograph plaque. Spin the center to reveal extra stars and butterflies, then hang it on the wall or display it on a shelf. It also comes with an Olivia Rodrigo minifigure dressed in a look from her Sour tour. Fisher-Price’s Rockin’ Record Player lets preschoolers spin toy records just like a real turntable. It comes with five records featuring 20 songs across country, pop, hip-hop, mindfulness and kids’ classics, plus a display rack to store them. It’s a fun, retro way for little music fans ages 3 and up to choose what they want to listen to on their own. This drum set allows kids ages 5 and older to choose from 20 drum styles, including rock, jazz and marching band, and play along with more than 30 built-in songs. Kids can also connect a phone via Bluetooth to drum along to their favorite music, record their performances and test their skills with three games and a coach mode. Want more from NBC Selected? articles.title: France's Macron blames protests on 'ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic'
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron blamed "ultra-left groups" for riots and looting as Paris businesses board up windows ahead of Saturday protests.
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron vowed Thursday to ban protests by "individuals or groups with no legitimate authority" as he blamed "ultra-left groups" for riots and looting that spread across his country. Macron made the remarks as thousands of protesters took to the streets of Paris on Thursday, according to The Associated Press, ahead of larger demonstrations set for this weekend. "Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic," Macron was quoted by Reuters as saying following a meeting with intelligence officials. The news agency reported that businesses in central Paris have started boarding up their windows over concerns of violence on Saturday. Local authorities also told Reuters that protests planned for Saturday in Lyon have been banned. FRANCE COULD FACE EVEN WORSE DESTRUCTION WITH SECOND WEEKEND OF PLANNED RIOTS, STATE DEPT WARNS Macron said the strategy adopted for the coming days is to ban protests requested by "individuals or groups with no legitimate authority." "Where trade unions submit requests to hold demonstrations, prefects will examine them in accordance with the law, but alternative routes will be proposed" to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings, Macron said. "The rules are simple, and I think they're just common sense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days," he said. "For those who still want to protest, if they are trade unions, prefects will propose alternative routes." Organizers of the Paris protest on Thursday said an administrative court in the city overturned a ban issued by police after they challenged it. The Paris police prefecture previously said the ban was necessary, given the risk of street violence after groups of masked youth clashed with police forces, looted shops and torched cars over the weekend. AMERICANS WARNED ABOUT PARIS TRAVEL AFTER VIOLENCE, LOOTING AND TEAR GAS-FILLED STREETS The protests began in France in September with calls for education reform, before expanding into larger anti-government demonstrations that French officials say are being fueled by far-left groups. Protesters gathered peacefully and chanted in the southeastern part of Paris on Thursday while they were watched by a heavy police presence, the AP reported. articles.title: I will make final decision on Rosebank oil field, energy secretary insists
articles.body:
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has insisted she will make the final decision over whether to approve the controversial Rosebank oil field, not the prime minister or chancellor.

She said there was a "tight" framework involved in making the decision to avoid it being overturned in the courts, and she was the only one who could make the final choice about whether to give the scheme the go-ahead.

Rosebank, which is about 80 miles (128km) north-west of Shetland, is Britain's largest untapped oil field and would also produce some gas.

Ministers said the decision would support the country's energy security with homegrown gas and protect jobs, while insisting it was also compatible with the UK's climate commitments.

But environmental campaigners have criticised the move, saying it will hamper efforts to tackle climate change and will have no meaningful impact on the UK's energy security or bills.

They argue Rosebank would be even more damaging for the environment than Jackdaw, as it would produce far more planet-warming greenhouse gases.

Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain

What is happening with the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields?

Fahnbulleh, who was previously a junior energy minister in Sir Keir Starmer's government, has been widely regarded in the past as being personally opposed to Rosebank.

Those in favour of the site's approval have been lobbying the Treasury hard in recent months to focus on the economic benefits of the site.

But Fahnbulleh made clear today that the decision would be made based on the legal requirements in the government's climate commitments.

Asked how much influence the Treasury had over her decision about Rosebank, Fahnbulleh told reporters at a lunch for political journalists in Westminster: "Ultimately, only I can make that decision.

"And I've really enjoyed reading bits in the media that [the prime minister] Andy's deciding this, [the chancellor] John's deciding that... actually only I can make that decision."

She described it as a "regulatory process not a policy process", governed by a set of tests she had to weigh the decision against.

Fahnbulleh said only a "tiny" number of people in her department had access to the documents involved in the decision-making process and would be aware of the choice she would make.

"You've got to read the documents and you've got to come to the right balance," she said, adding that she would weigh factors like its impact on the climate as well as economic considerations like jobs and economic growth.

"It sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because in the end only I can make it," Fahnbulleh said.

"And if it is overturned by other colleagues, all that means is we're going to be overturned in the courts. So we will do the process and we will do it properly."

The decision over Rosebank is more difficult politically for the government than Jackdaw.

While most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

Fahnbulleh acknowledged this in an interview with the BBC on Wednesday, saying Rosebank was a "different proposition" to Jackdaw as the oil will be exported.

Licences for both fields were granted by the then Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023 - sparking legal challenges from environmental groups.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

It was then for the UK government to decide whether to re-approve the fields, with input from industry regulators.

Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.
